answer.short:
$-\frac{x}{y}$

Rewrite the negative powers as reciprocals, then cancel the common factor.

$\frac1{x^2}-\frac1{y^2}$

Use the difference of two squares.

$\frac{3x^2y^2}{x+y}$

Combine the reciprocal terms before dividing.

Combine each sum of reciprocals, then divide.

$\frac{x^4}{1+2x^2y+x^4y^2}$

Combine the terms, take the reciprocal and square.

$\frac{x^2y}{x^2+y}$

Combine the reciprocal terms, then take the reciprocal.

content.prompt: At the beginning of 2011, the population of Australia was estimated to be approximately 22.5 million. If the population stayed the same for the next year, and each person in Australia produced an average of 0.712 kg of waste each day, how many tonnes of waste would be produced by Australians in the following year? answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Annual waste}&=(2.25\times10^7)\times0.712\times365\text{ kg}\\\text{Annual waste}&=5.8473\times10^9\text{ kg}\\\text{Annual waste}&=\frac{5.8473\times10^9}{10^3}\text{ tonnes}\\\text{Annual waste}&=5.8473\times10^6\text{ tonnes}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A light year is the distance light travels in a year. Light travels at approximately $3\times10^5$ km/s. Use 1 year = 365 days.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How wide is our galaxy (in kilometres) if it is approximately 230 000 light years across? Give your answer in scientific notation, correct to three significant figures.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Seconds in a year}&=365\times24\times60\times60\\\text{Seconds in a year}&=3.1536\times10^7\\\text{Galaxy width}&=(2.3\times10^5)(3\times10^5)(3.1536\times10^7)\text{ km}\\\text{Galaxy width}&=2.175984\times10^{18}\text{ km}\\\text{Galaxy width}&\approx2.18\times10^{18}\text{ km}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: How far from us (in kilometres) is the farthest galaxy detected by optical telescopes if it is approximately $13\times10^9$ light years from us? Give your answer in scientific notation, correct to three significant figures.

children.label: c
children.prompt: How long does it take light to travel from the Sun to the Earth if the distance between the Sun and the Earth is $1.4951\times10^8$ km? Give your answer in minutes and seconds, correct to the nearest second.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{d}{v}\\t&=\frac{1.4951\times10^8}{3\times10^5}\text{ s}\\t&=\frac{14951}{30}\text{ s}\\t&\approx498\text{ s}\end{align*}$$

Since $498=8\times60+18$, the time is approximately 8 minutes 18 seconds.

teachingContext.mappingNote: Parts a–b multiply speed by the number of seconds in the stated light-year distances; part c divides distance by speed. The definition and speed are supplied in the question.

content.prompt: The mass of a hydrogen atom is approximately $1.674\times10^{-27}$ kg and the mass of an electron is approximately $9.1\times10^{-31}$ kg. How many electrons, correct to the nearest whole number, will it take to equal the mass of a single hydrogen atom?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}N&=\frac{1.674\times10^{-27}}{9.1\times10^{-31}}\\N&=\frac{1.674}{9.1}\times10^4\\N&=\frac{167400}{91}\\N&\approx1840\end{align*}$$

Approximately 1840 electrons have the mass of one hydrogen atom.

inlines.text: Prove that the index laws hold for negative integer exponents. (Use the laws for positive integer exponents.)
For example, the product-of-powers result can be proved in the following way for negative integer exponents.

answer.short:
For non-zero bases, all five laws hold: $a^{-p}a^{-q}=a^{-(p+q)}$, $\dfrac{a^{-p}}{a^{-q}}=a^{q-p}$, $(a^{-p})^{-q}=a^{pq}$, $(ab)^{-p}=a^{-p}b^{-p}$ and $\left(\dfrac ab\right)^{-p}=\dfrac{a^{-p}}{b^{-p}}$.

Replace negative powers by reciprocals and use the positive-integer laws.
answer.worked:
Let $a,b\ne0$ and let $p,q$ be positive integers. Use $a^{-p}=1/a^p$.

Product:
$$\begin{aligned}a^{-p}a^{-q}&=\frac1{a^p}\frac1{a^q}\\a^{-p}a^{-q}&=\frac1{a^{p+q}}\\a^{-p}a^{-q}&=a^{-(p+q)}=a^{-p+(-q)}.\end{aligned}$$
Quotient:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a^{-p}}{a^{-q}}&=\frac{1/a^p}{1/a^q}\\\frac{a^{-p}}{a^{-q}}&=\frac{a^q}{a^p}\\\frac{a^{-p}}{a^{-q}}&=a^{q-p}=a^{-p-(-q)}.\end{aligned}$$
Here cancellation gives $a^{q-p}$ when $q\ge p$, and $1/a^{p-q}=a^{q-p}$ when $q<p$.

Power of a power:
$$\begin{aligned}(a^{-p})^{-q}&=\frac1{(a^{-p})^q}\\(a^{-p})^{-q}&=\frac1{(1/a^p)^q}\\(a^{-p})^{-q}&=a^{pq}=a^{(-p)(-q)}.\end{aligned}$$
Power of a product:
$$\begin{aligned}(ab)^{-p}&=\frac1{(ab)^p}\\(ab)^{-p}&=\frac1{a^pb^p}\\(ab)^{-p}&=a^{-p}b^{-p}.\end{aligned}$$
Power of a quotient:
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac ab\right)^{-p}&=\frac1{(a/b)^p}\\\left(\frac ab\right)^{-p}&=\frac{b^p}{a^p}\\\left(\frac ab\right)^{-p}&=\frac{a^{-p}}{b^{-p}}.\end{aligned}$$

inlines.text: Prove that the index laws hold for fractional exponents.
can be proved in the following way.
The result can easily be extended to

answer.short:
For $a,b>0$ and rational $r,s$, $a^ra^s=a^{r+s}$, $\dfrac{a^r}{a^s}=a^{r-s}$, $(a^r)^s=a^{rs}$, $(ab)^r=a^rb^r$ and $\left(\dfrac ab\right)^r=\dfrac{a^r}{b^r}$.

Write fractional powers as roots and use integer index laws; positive roots are unique.
answer.worked:
Let $a,b>0$, $r=p/n$ and $s=q/m$, where $p,q$ are integers and $n,m$ are positive integers. Put $c=\sqrt[nm]{a}$. Then $a^r=c^{pm}$ and $a^s=c^{qn}$ by the definition of rational powers.

Product:
$$\begin{aligned}a^ra^s&=c^{pm}c^{qn}\\a^ra^s&=c^{pm+qn}\\a^ra^s&=a^{(pm+qn)/(nm)}\\a^ra^s&=a^{r+s}.\end{aligned}$$
Quotient:
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=\frac{c^{pm}}{c^{qn}}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=c^{pm-qn}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=a^{(pm-qn)/(nm)}\\\frac{a^r}{a^s}&=a^{r-s}.\end{aligned}$$
Power of a power: let $d=\sqrt[n]{a}$ and $z=(a^{p/n})^{q/m}$. The definition of an $m$th root gives $z^m=(d^p)^q$; hence
$$\begin{aligned}z^{mn}&=((d^p)^q)^n\\z^{mn}&=d^{pqn}\\z^{mn}&=a^{pq}.\end{aligned}$$
Since $z>0$, uniqueness of the positive $mn$th root gives
$$\begin{aligned}(a^{p/n})^{q/m}&=a^{pq/(mn)}\\(a^r)^s&=a^{rs}.\end{aligned}$$
For the remaining laws put $u=\sqrt[n]{a}$ and $v=\sqrt[n]{b}$. Since $(uv)^n=ab$ and $(u/v)^n=a/b$, uniqueness of positive roots gives $\sqrt[n]{ab}=uv$ and $\sqrt[n]{a/b}=u/v$.

Power of a product:
$$\begin{aligned}(ab)^{p/n}&=(uv)^p\\(ab)^{p/n}&=u^pv^p\\(ab)^{p/n}&=a^{p/n}b^{p/n}.\end{aligned}$$
Power of a quotient:
$$\begin{aligned}\left(\frac ab\right)^{p/n}&=\left(\frac uv\right)^p\\\left(\frac ab\right)^{p/n}&=\frac{u^p}{v^p}\\\left(\frac ab\right)^{p/n}&=\frac{a^{p/n}}{b^{p/n}}.\end{aligned}$$
The integer laws include negative numerators by part a, so these arguments also cover negative fractional exponents.

Many mathematical problems have exact answers, such as \(\frac{13}{7}\), \(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}\) or \(400\pi\). However, in the real world, very large numbers and very small numbers are common and, nearly always, these can only be determined approximately. To express large and small numbers conveniently, we use scientific notation, also known as standard form.

entries.description:
Every time we record a physical measurement, we write down an approximation to the ‘true value’. For example, we may say that a standard A4 sheet of paper is 30 cm by 21 cm. This has a conventional meaning and says that the actual length is between 29.5 cm and 30.5 cm. If we measure the sheet of paper more accurately, we could say that it is 29.7 cm × 21.0 cm. This means that we believe that the actual length is between 29.65 cm and 29.75 cm. Similarly, if we say a girl’s height is 156 cm to the nearest centimetre, this means that her actual height is between 155.5 and 156.5 cm.

In this situation, we say that a measurement recorded as 156 cm is correct to three significant figures. Similarly, when we say that the width of the paper is 21 cm, this is correct to two significant figures.

Using approximations of π as another example, we say that 3.14 is π correct to three significant figures and 3.14159 is π correct to six significant figures. When we round a number, we record it correct to a certain number of significant figures.

The rules for rounding require you to first identify the last significant digit. Then:
• if the next digit is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4, round down
• if the next digit is 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9, round up.

So π = 3.141592654 … is rounded to 3, 3.1, 3.14, 3.142, 3.1416, 3.14159, 3.141593 and so on, depending on the number of significant figures required.

We use the symbol ≈ to mean that two numbers are approximately equal to each other.

entries.description:
We begin by considering what we mean by powers such as \(3^{1/2}\), \(2^{1/3}\) and \(\pi^{1/10}\), in which the exponent is the reciprocal of a positive integer.
Recall that if \(a\) is positive, \(\sqrt a\) is the positive number whose square is \(a\). That is:
\((\sqrt a)^2=a=a^1\).
For this reason, we introduce an alternative notation for \(\sqrt a\): we write it as \(a^{1/2}\). We do this because then we preserve the third index law:
\((a^{1/2})^2=a^{2\times1/2}=a^1\).
Keep in mind that \(a^{1/2}\) is nothing more than an alternative notation for \(\sqrt a\).

Similarly, every positive number \(a\) has a cube root, \(\sqrt[3]a\). It is the positive number whose cube is \(a\); that is, \((\sqrt[3]a)^3=a=a^1\).

\((a^{1/3})^3=a^{3\times1/3}=a^1\).
The same can be done for \(\sqrt[4]a\), \(\sqrt[5]a\) and so on. The alternative notations are:
\(\sqrt[4]a=a^{1/4},\ \sqrt[5]a=a^{1/5}\) and so on.

The five index laws introduced previously for integer indices are equally valid for rational indices. This follows from the definition of a^x, where x is rational.
We will leave a discussion of the proofs of these laws to the Challenge exercises.

This means that when we evaluate a^{p/q}, it does not matter if we take the qth root first and the pth power second, or the pth power first and the qth power second. For example:
4^{3/2} = (4^{1/2})^3 = 2^3 = 8
and also:

entries.description:
Key features:
• y = 2^x is an increasing function; that is, 2^x increases as x increases.
• A y-intercept occurs at (0, 1) but there is no x-intercept.
• As x moves away from 0 in the negative direction (to the left), the value of 2^x gets close to 0, but it never equals 0. Why? We say that the x-axis is an asymptote for the graph of y = 2^x.

paragraphs: From the previous section, we have seen that the graph of y = 2^x is increasing and the graph of y = 2^{-x} = (1/2)^x is decreasing.

In general, suppose that a is a positive number different from 1. Since the graphs of y = a^x are either increasing or decreasing (unless a = 1), there is only one value of x for each value of y. Hence, we know that if a^c = a^d, then c = d.

In the following examples, this fact is used to solve exponential equations. From the above discussion it can be seen that there is only one solution for x to the equation a^x = y, provided that y is positive.

entries.description:
The first example is a mathematical model of the number of bacteria in a culture.
Initially, there are 1000 bacteria in a culture. The number of bacteria is doubling every hour.
Therefore:
• after 1 hour there are 1000 × 2 bacteria
• after 2 hours there are 1000 × 2 × 2 = 1000 × 2² bacteria
• after 3 hours there are 1000 × 2² × 2 = 1000 × 2³ bacteria.
Following this pattern, there are 1000 × 2ᵗ bacteria after t hours. This can be written as a formula.
Let N be the number of bacteria after t hours. Then:
N = 1000 × 2ᵗ
A graph can be plotted by first producing a table of values.

For example, the product-of-powers result can be proved in the following way for negative integer exponents.
